reasoning: Both are strong, opinionated strategy memos with real self-criticism, and neither builds its central recommendation on a false premise. B wins on verification depth and source honesty. I checked the load-bearing claims against primary sources. B's decisive facts are exact: Figma's own FAQ says 'If you have a Full seat on the Professional, Organization, or Enterprise plans, you can use the agent in all your files. Users with a View, Collab, or Dev seat can try it in Draft files'; the agent is 'free to use during the beta. AI credits are not consumed', with credits applying at GA; beta rollout began 20 May 2026 in waves; the agent generates from connected libraries' components, styles and variables as real editable layers; Figma Sites publishing requires a paid plan and a Full seat; and Q1 2026 revenue of $333.4M, +46% YoY, with NDR of 139% (highest in over two years) matches Figma's own Q1 2026 earnings release filed with the SEC. B's whole recommendation rests on that seat gate and the coming meter, and both are verified. B also grades its own sources ('treat the launch mechanics and seat tiers as well-corroborated, the revenue figures as single-source, and the designer-sentiment survey as an incumbent self-report') and discounts the 91% figure in-text as 'a vibe reading, not evidence' - that stat is real (Figma's State of the Designer 2026, n=906) and is indeed the incumbent surveying its own users, so B's labeling is accurate and appropriately conservative. B has three real errors, all peripheral and all tilting toward its own thesis: it says the Starter plan is 'excluded outright' when Figma's FAQ states the agent IS available on Starter; it dates Canva AI 2.0 to March 2026 when it launched at Canva Create on 15-16 April 2026 (the substance - a proprietary design-specific foundation model, Canva owning the non-designer relationship - is verified); and 'shared libraries live on Organization and Enterprise' is imprecise, since component library publishing is available on Professional and above. None of these unseats the core argument, because the paying-company motion B is reasoning about sits on Professional/Org/Enterprise, where the gate is exactly as described. A is accurate on everything it asserts - agent native to canvas producing real artboards, agent quality dependent on an existing design system, Figma Sites publishing responsive sites with a CMS, Figma Make going prompt-to-app all check out - but it asserts far less and never checks access or pricing at all. That omission is load-bearing here. A's most emphatic verified claim is that Figma is 'already at the destination' and therefore the 'our output is live, we're safe' argument 'will get checked and it will fall over'; in fact Figma Sites publishing requires a paid plan and a Full seat, so A is warning its reader off an argument that is partly correct for A's own segment. Likewise A's central framing that prompt-to-screen 'dissolves the interface barrier for everyone at once' is materially weakened by a fact A never looked up: in real design files the agent is Full-seat-gated, and the non-designer is precisely the person on a Collab or View seat. A also presents a personal blog (sanjaytarani.com) as 'independent testing' and stamps it 'Confirmed' without any source-strength labeling, on the claim it calls 'the single most important fact in this document' - the claim happens to be corroborated by Figma's own docs, but the sourcing is weaker than advertised. On breadth, B covers more genuinely distinct angles: launch mechanics stripped of narrative, the business-model read (NDR 139% as an expansion instrument), the threat reframe (consolidation, not capability), winners/losers including a non-obvious party, first/second/third-order effects culminating in 'design system contamination', two historical analogies deliberately pointing in opposite directions, bear cases against both Figma and the reader, and a named adjacent threat (Canva) that A misses entirely. A's structure is cleaner and its Section 5 sequencing with pre-committed kill criteria is the single best passage in either document - more falsifiable than B's 90-day plan. B also carries a visible production defect: an unfilled template placeholder, '[SKILL]', leaks into the text at the risk-versus-impact list. I could not independently verify B's characterisation of 'complaints already visible about Figma Make's credit limits' beyond its being a plausible secondary-source read, and I did not find confirmation that Figma Sites carries a CMS-only Content seat exception relevant to either argument beyond noting it exists. Net: B is the more decision-useful memo because the facts a reader would act on are the ones it got right, while A's caution is purchased by not checking.
